sentences.t:
Cwōm þā tō flōde felamōdigra,
hægstealdra [hēap]; hringnet bǣron,
locene leoðosyrcan.
sentences.l: There came then to the flood a troop of the very bold, of young warriors; they bore ring-net, linked limb-corslets.
sentences.i: Then a band of bold young warriors came down to the shore; they wore mail, corslets of linked rings.
sentences.n: ‘Cwōm’ is the singular past of ‘cuman’, ‘came’, and its subject is ‘[hēap]’, ‘troop’, a noun that the manuscript lacks and Grein supplied: ‘felamōdigra’ (‘of the very bold’, from ‘fela’ ‘much’ and ‘mōdig’ ‘spirited’) and ‘hægstealdra’ (‘of young warriors’; a ‘hægsteald’ is a young unmarried man, a fighting man) are genitive plurals and need a noun to hang on. ‘bǣron’ is a plural past, ‘bore, wore’, so the verb agrees with the men the troop is made of; the manuscript spells it ‘bæron’, and Sievers (with a query) and Trautmann read the infinitive ‘beran’, Holthausen ‘beron’, after ‘cwōm’, ‘came to bear’. ‘tō flōde’ is ‘to the water’, the shore where the ship lies (1896). ‘hringnet’ is ‘ring-net’, a mail-coat of linked rings, first met here, and ‘locene leoðosyrcan’ says it again as ‘linked limb-corslets’: ‘leoðosyrce’ is a shirt that covers the limbs (‘leoðu’ ‘limbs’ and ‘syrce’ ‘shirt, byrnie’), and ‘locene’ is the past participle of ‘lūcan’, ‘lock, link’.

sentences.t:
Landweard onfand
eftsīð eorla, swā hē ǣr dyde;
sentences.l: The land-guard found out the earls’ return-journey, as he had done before;
sentences.i: The coast-guard saw the earls coming back, as he had seen them come the first time;
sentences.n: ‘Landweard onfand eftsīð eorla’ is ‘the land-guard found out the earls’ return-journey’: ‘onfand’ is the past of ‘onfindan’, ‘find out, perceive’, ‘eftsīð’ (‘eft’ ‘again, back’ and ‘sīð’ ‘journey’) is its object, and ‘eorla’ a genitive plural, ‘of the earls’. The ‘Landweard’ is the Danish watchman of the cliffs, the ‘coast-guard’ of the earlier notes, who saw the Geats arrive and questioned them (229–257); ‘swā hē ǣr dyde’, ‘as he did before’, points back to that, with ‘dyde’ (past of ‘dōn’) standing in for ‘onfand’.

sentences.t:
nō hē mid hearme of hliðes nōsan
gæs(tas) grētte, ac him tōgēanes rād,
sentences.l: not he with harm from the cliff’s nose greeted the guests, but rode to meet them,
sentences.i: He did not hail the guests with any hostility from the headland’s brow, but rode down to meet them,
sentences.n: ‘nō hē … grētte’ is ‘he did not greet’, ‘grētte’ being the past of ‘grētan’, and its object is ‘gæs(tas)’, ‘guests’, an accusative plural: the parentheses mark the ending ‘-tas’, restored where the manuscript is lost (leaf 171b shows ‘gæs’ and then a gap, and Grundtvig reads ‘gæstas’). ‘mid hearme’ is ‘with harm’, ‘hearme’ a dative of ‘hearm’, ‘hurt, insult’ (Trautmann reads ‘hrēame’, ‘with an outcry’). ‘of hliðes nōsan’ is ‘from the cliff’s nose’: ‘hlið’ is a slope or cliff and ‘nōse’ a nose, here a jutting headland, from which the watchman would have looked down. ‘ac him tōgēanes rād’ is ‘but rode to meet them’, with ‘him’ a dative and ‘tōgēanes’ coming after it. The clause sets this friendly meeting against the stern questions he put at 237–257.

sentences.t:
cwæð þæt wilcuman Wedera lēodum
scaþan scīrhame tō scipe fōron.
sentences.l: said that welcome-comers to the Weders’ people, scathers bright-coated, were faring to the ship.
sentences.i: and said that the Weders’ people, welcome guests in shining mail, were on their way to their ship.
sentences.n: ‘cwæð’ is ‘said’, and the ‘þæt’ clause gives his words, with ‘fōron’ the plural past of ‘faran’, ‘fared, went’, and ‘tō scipe’ ‘to the ship’. ‘wilcuman’ is a nominative plural, ‘welcome ones’ (‘wil-’ ‘pleasure’ and ‘cuma’ ‘comer’), followed by ‘Wedera lēodum’, a dative plural, ‘to the Weders’ people’. Taken word for word that says ‘welcome-comers to the Weders’ people’, and the grammar does not settle who is welcoming whom. Grein changed ‘lēodum’ to the nominative ‘lēode’ (the form at 225, ‘Wedera lēode’), which would make the guests the Weders themselves; ‘i’ gives that sense, and treating Klaeber’s dative as a loose one is a guess. ‘scaþan scīrhame’ is ‘scathers bright-coated’: ‘scaþa’ means ‘injurer, foe, raider’, and for a band of armed men ‘warriors’ is a guess from the context, while ‘scīrhame’ (‘scīr’ ‘bright’ and ‘hama’ ‘covering, coat’) occurs only here and means in shining mail. The manuscript letters after ‘sca’ are lost: one of the 1787 transcripts has ‘scawan’ and the other ‘scaþan’, and Grein’s choice of ‘scaþan’ is printed.

sentences.l: Then was on the sand the sea-roomy boat laden with war-garments, the ring-prowed one, with horses and with treasures;
sentences.i: Then the roomy sea-ship with its ringed prow stood on the sand, loaded with war-gear, with horses and with treasures;
sentences.n: ‘Þā wæs on sande … naca hladen’ is ‘then the boat was laden on the sand’: ‘naca’ is a nominative, ‘hladen’ the past participle of ‘hladan’, ‘load’, and ‘wæs … hladen’ makes the passive. ‘sǣgēap’ is ‘sea-roomy’ (‘sǣ’ ‘sea’ and ‘gēap’ ‘wide, spacious’); the poem has it nowhere else, so ‘roomy’ rests on the lexica. ‘hringedstefna’ is the ‘ring-prowed one’ of 32 and 1131, in apposition to ‘naca’. ‘herewǣdum’ (‘war-garments’, that is armour and war-gear), ‘mēarum’ (‘horses’) and ‘māðmum’ (‘treasures’) are datives plural of what it is loaded with, and the horses and treasures are Hrothgar’s gifts (compare 1035 and 1046).

sentences.t:
mæst hlīfade
ofer Hrōðgāres hordgestrēonum.
sentences.l: The mast towered over Hrothgar’s hoard-treasures.
sentences.i: The mast rose high above Hrothgar’s treasures from the hoard.
sentences.n: ‘mæst hlīfade’ is ‘the mast towered’; ‘hlīfade’ is the past of ‘hlīfian’, ‘rise high’, the verb used of the hall at 81 (‘Sele hlīfade’). ‘ofer’ takes the dative here, ‘hordgestrēonum’, ‘over the hoard-treasures’ (‘hord’ ‘hoard’ and ‘gestrēon’ ‘gain, treasure’), so the heaped gifts of Hrothgar’s hoard lie in the ship and the mast stands up above them.

sentences.t:
Hē þǣm bātwearde bunden golde
swurd gesealde, þæt hē syðþan wæs
on meodubence māþme þȳ weorþra,
yrfelāfe.
sentences.l: He gave to that boat-guard a sword bound with gold, so that he afterwards was on the mead-bench the worthier by that treasure, an heirloom.
sentences.i: He gave the guardian of the boat a sword bound with gold, so that from then on he stood higher in honour on the mead-bench for that treasure, an heirloom.
sentences.n: The first ‘Hē’ is Beowulf, who gives (‘gesealde’, past of ‘sellan’) a sword to ‘þǣm bātwearde’, ‘that boat-guard’ (‘bāt’ ‘boat’ and ‘weard’ ‘guard’), a dative; the second ‘hē’ in the ‘þæt’ clause is the boat-guard, so the subject changes in mid-sentence. ‘bunden golde’ is ‘bound with gold’, a participle with a dative of means, describing the sword; what part of it is bound with gold is not said, and a gold-bound hilt would be a guess. The guard is probably the Dane who watched the ship, of whom the coast-guard spoke at 293–296; the lines do not say whether he is the coast-guard himself or one of his young men. ‘þæt hē syðþan wæs … māþme þȳ weorþra’ is ‘so that he was afterwards the worthier by the treasure’: ‘þȳ’ is an instrumental ‘by that’ before a comparative, ‘weorþra’ the comparative of ‘weorþ’, ‘honoured, worthy’, and ‘meodubenc’ is the ‘mead-bench’, the bench in the hall where men sat and drank, so he gains standing among drinking-companions. ‘yrfelāfe’ is ‘as an heirloom’ (‘yrfe’ ‘inheritance’ and ‘lāf’ ‘what is left’), standing in apposition to ‘swurd’ or to ‘māþme’; the ending does not tell which. Klaeber’s italic letters mark two changes: the manuscript has ‘maþma’ and ‘weorþre’ (the first would be a genitive plural, ‘of treasures’, and the second an ending that does not suit a masculine ‘hē’), and Thorkelin’s ‘māþme’ and ‘weorþra’ are printed, so that both words agree with what the clause needs.

sentences.t:
Gewāt him on naca
drēfan dēop wæter, Dena land ofgeaf.
sentences.l: The boat went itself on, to stir the deep water; it gave up the Danes’ land.
sentences.i: The ship stood out to sea, churning the deep water, and left the land of the Danes behind.
sentences.n: ‘Gewāt him on naca’ is ‘the boat went (itself) on’: ‘him’ is a reflexive dative, ‘on’ here an adverb, ‘onward’, and ‘naca’ the nominative subject, which also serves for ‘ofgeaf’ (past of ‘ofgiefan’, ‘give up, leave’), ‘left the Danes’ land’, ‘Dena’ a genitive plural. ‘drēfan’ is an infinitive of purpose after a verb of motion, ‘to drive, stir’, with ‘dēop wæter’ ‘deep water’ as object. The italic final ‘a’ in ‘naca’ marks a change: the manuscript has ‘nacan’, which would be an oblique case, ‘in the boat’, and leave ‘drēfan’ without a subject. Grein printed ‘[ȳð]nacan’, ‘wave-boat’, Rieger and three editors ‘naca’ as Klaeber does, Sedgefield ‘[eft] on nacan’, and Bugge supposed that two half-lines are lost before ‘gewāt’.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs be mæste merehrægla sum,
segl sāle fæst;
sentences.l: Then was by the mast a certain one of the sea-garments, a sail fast to its rope;
sentences.i: By the mast there was a sail, a sea-garment, made fast to its rope;
sentences.n: ‘merehrægla sum’ is ‘a certain one of the sea-garments’: ‘sum’ is ‘a certain one’ and takes the genitive plural ‘merehrægla’, and ‘merehrægl’ (‘mere’ ‘sea’ and ‘hrægl’ ‘garment’) is a kenning for the sail, first met here, which clothes the mast as a garment clothes a man; ‘segl’ in the next line says the same in plain words. ‘be mæste’ is ‘by the mast’, ‘be’ with a dative. ‘sāle fæst’ is ‘fast to a rope’, ‘sāle’ a dative of ‘sāl’, ‘rope’ (as in ‘on sāle’ at 302).

sentences.l: The sound-wood boomed; not there did the wind over the waves deprive the wave-floater of its journey;
sentences.i: The ship’s timbers boomed, and on that voyage the wind over the waves did not hold the vessel back;
sentences.n: ‘sundwudu’ is the ‘sound-wood’ of 208, the ship, and ‘þunede’ the past of ‘þunian’, which the lexica give as ‘thunder, resound, make a loud noise’; the picture of the timbers booming and creaking under a good wind is my reading and a guess. ‘nō þǣr … sīðes getwǣfde’ is ‘there the wind did not rob it of its journey’: ‘getwǣfde’ is the past of ‘getwǣfan’, ‘part from, deprive’, which takes the genitive of what is taken away, here ‘sīðes’ (‘of the journey’), with ‘wēgflotan’ a dative, ‘the wave-floater’, a kenning for the ship (‘flota’ ‘floater’, as at 210 and 218, and ‘wēg-’ the Anglian spelling of ‘wǣg’ ‘wave’, as I take it). ‘wind ofer ȳðum’ is ‘the wind over the waves’, ‘ȳðum’ a dative plural.

sentences.t:
sǣgenga fōr,
flēat fāmigheals forð ofer ȳðe,
bundenstefna ofer brimstrēamas,
sentences.l: The sea-goer fared, foamy-necked it floated forth over the wave, the bound-prowed one over the sea-streams,
sentences.i: The ship sailed on, foam at its neck, floating forth over the waves, its bound prow riding the streams of the sea,
sentences.n: ‘sǣgenga’ is the ‘sea-goer’ of 1882, the ship, subject of ‘fōr’ (past of ‘faran’) and of ‘flēat’ (past of ‘flēotan’, ‘float’). ‘fāmigheals’ is ‘foamy-necked’ (‘fāmig’ ‘foamy’ and ‘heals’ ‘neck’), the ‘fāmīheals’ of 218, where the neck was taken as the curve of the bow throwing spray, a guess. ‘bundenstefna’ is ‘bound-prowed’ (‘bunden’ ‘bound’ and ‘stefna’ ‘prow’), probably a ship whose stem is held together with lashings, though the picture is a guess; compare ‘wundenstefna’ at 220. ‘ofer ȳðe’ is ‘over the wave’, with a singular form of ‘ȳð’ after ‘ofer’, and ‘brimstrēamas’ are the ‘sea-streams’ (‘brim’ ‘sea’ and ‘strēam’ ‘stream’), the currents of open water.

sentences.t:
þæt hīe Gēata clifu ongitan meahton,
cūþe næssas;
sentences.l: so that they could perceive the Geats’ cliffs, the known headlands;
sentences.i: until they could make out the cliffs of the Geats, the headlands they knew;
sentences.n: The ‘þæt’ clause says how far the ship ran: ‘þæt hīe … ongitan meahton’ is ‘so that they could perceive’, ‘ongitan’ an infinitive, ‘perceive, see’, and ‘meahton’ a plural past of ‘magan’, which is the same in the indicative and the subjunctive. ‘Gēata clifu’ is ‘the cliffs of the Geats’ (‘Gēata’ a genitive plural, ‘clifu’ a neuter accusative plural), and ‘cūþe næssas’ ‘the known headlands’ (‘cūþ’ ‘known’; ‘næs’ ‘headland, ness’), in apposition.

sentences.t:
cēol ūp geþrang
lyftgeswenced, on lande stōd.
sentences.l: The keel pressed up, air-driven; on land it stood.
sentences.i: The ship, driven on by the wind, ran up the shore and stood on land.
sentences.n: ‘cēol’ is ‘keel’, standing for the whole ship, as in the ‘cēol’ of 238. ‘ūp geþrang’ is ‘pressed up’: ‘geþrang’ is the past of ‘geþringan’, ‘press, throng, force a way’, and ‘ūp’ means up the beach. ‘lyftgeswenced’ is ‘air-driven’ (‘lyft’ ‘air’ and ‘geswenced’, past participle of ‘swencan’, ‘afflict, drive’), the wind that carried it in; the compound is found only here, and Trautmann would read ‘lyfte’ as a separate dative, ‘by the air’. ‘on lande stōd’ is ‘stood on land’, aground on the beach; Sievers, Holthausen and Sedgefield add ‘þæt hē’ before it, which turns it into a clause, ‘so that it stood on land’, and Klaeber leaves the half-line without it.

sentences.l: Quickly was at the water the harbour-guard ready, he who for a long time before, eager at the shore, gazed far for the dear men;
sentences.i: The harbour-guard was quickly at the water’s edge, ready, he who had long been looking far out from the shore, eager for his dear men;
sentences.n: ‘Hraþe wæs … hȳðweard geara’ is ‘quickly was the harbour-guard ready’: ‘hraþe’ is ‘quickly’ (the manuscript has ‘hreþe’, corrected to ‘hraþe’), ‘æt holme’ ‘at the water’ (‘holm’ ‘sea, water’), and ‘hȳðweard’ (‘hȳð’ ‘harbour’ and ‘weard’ ‘guard’) is found only here. ‘geara’ I take as the adjective ‘ready’, the ‘gearo’ of 121 in another spelling, nominative singular masculine; this is a guess, since ‘geara’ is also the adverb ‘of old’. This is the Geat watchman at home, who waits for his own people, where the Danish ‘Landweard’ of 1890 watched for strangers. ‘sē þe ǣr lange tīd … wlātode’ is ‘who for a long time before gazed’, ‘lange tīd’ an accusative of time, ‘wlātode’ the past of ‘wlātian’, ‘look’, with ‘feor’ ‘far’ and ‘fūs’ ‘eager’ (nominative, describing him); ‘lēofra manna’ is a genitive plural, ‘of dear men’, the people he looked out for, and ‘æt faroðe’ ‘at the shore’ (‘faroð’ ‘shore, shore-water’).

sentences.t:
sǣlde tō sande sīdfæþme scip
oncẹrbendum fæst, þȳ lǣs hym ȳþa ðrym
wudu wynsuman forwrecan meahte.
sentences.l: He moored to the sand the broad-bosomed ship, fast with anchor-bonds, lest the force of the waves might wreck the pleasant wood for them.
sentences.i: He made the broad-bosomed ship fast to the sand with anchor-ropes, so that the surge of the waves could not wreck the lovely timbers.
sentences.n: ‘sǣlde’ is the past of ‘sǣlan’, ‘fasten with a rope’ (‘sǣwudu sǣldon’ at 226), with ‘scip’ as its object and ‘tō sande’ ‘to the sand’; the subject is the harbour-guard, carried over from the last unit. ‘sīdfæþme’ is ‘broad-bosomed’ (‘sīd’ ‘wide’ and ‘fæþm’ ‘embrace, bosom’), the ‘sīdfæþmed scip’ of 302, which the note there calls a guess at ‘roomy’. ‘oncẹrbendum’ is ‘with anchor-bonds’, the cables, a dative plural, ‘oncer’ being the loan-word ‘ancor’ (the ‘ancre’ of 1883). The dot under the ‘e’ is Klaeber’s sign that this vowel does not count in the metre, so the verse is scanned as if it were missing. His italic ‘e’ marks a change, since the manuscript has ‘oncear’ and Grundtvig’s transcript ‘oncer-’. ‘þȳ lǣs’ is ‘lest’ and takes the subjunctive ‘meahte’ (the past singular of ‘magan’ looks the same in the indicative, so the mood comes from the conjunction); ‘ȳþa ðrym’ is ‘the force of waves’ (‘ȳþa’ a genitive plural, ‘þrym’ ‘force, might’), the subject, and ‘wudu wynsuman’ ‘the pleasant wood’, the ship, its object, ‘wynsum’ meaning ‘pleasant, delightful’. ‘forwrecan’ I take as ‘wreck, dash to pieces’ from the lexica’s ‘drive to destruction’. ‘hym’ is ‘him’ in another spelling, a dative of interest that is singular or plural (‘him’ serves for both), so it may mean the crew or the ship; ‘l’ renders it ‘for them’ and ‘i’ leaves it out.

sentences.t:
Hēt þā ūp beran æþelinga gestrēon,
frætwe ond fǣtgold;
sentences.l: He bade then bear up the athelings’ treasure, the trappings and plate-gold;
sentences.i: Then he ordered the princes’ treasure carried up from the ship, the fine trappings and the gold plate;
sentences.n: ‘Hēt … beran’ is ‘bade bear’: ‘hēt’ takes an infinitive, and the men who carry it are left unnamed, so the object ‘æþelinga gestrēon’, ‘the athelings’ treasure’, stands next to the verb; the subject of ‘Hēt’ is not stated and changes from the harbour-guard of ‘sǣlde’; ‘him’ in the next line is the traveller bound for Higelac, so Beowulf is understood. ‘æþelinga’ is a genitive plural, ‘of the princes, nobles’, and ‘gestrēon’ ‘treasure’. ‘frætwe’ is an accusative plural, ‘trappings, ornaments’, and ‘fǣtgold’ is ‘plate-gold’ (‘fǣt’ ‘vessel, plate’): the word occurs only here, and I take it as gold made into vessels or plates, which is a guess. ‘ūp’ means up from the ship onto the shore.

sentences.t:
næs him feor þanon
tō gesēcanne sinces bryttan,
Higelāc Hrēþling, þǣr æt hām wunað
selfa mid gesīðum sǣwealle nēah.
sentences.l: It was not far for him from there to seek the dispenser of treasure, Higelac the Hrethling, where at home he dwells himself with his companions near the sea-wall.
sentences.i: It was not far for him from there to Higelac, son of Hrethel, the giver of treasure, who lives there at home himself with his companions, close by the sea-wall.
sentences.n: ‘næs him feor þanon tō gesēcanne …’ is ‘it was not far for him from there to seek …’: ‘næs’ is ‘ne wæs’, ‘him’ a dative, and ‘tō gesēcanne’ an inflected infinitive, ‘to seek’. ‘sinces bryttan’ is ‘dispenser of treasure’, ‘bryttan’ an accusative of ‘bryta’, ‘dispenser’, a stock title for a lord (‘sinces brytta’ at 607), and ‘Higelāc Hrēþling’ stands beside it: ‘Hrēþling’ is ‘son of Hrethel’, the ending ‘-ling’ marking descent from Hrethel (374). ‘þǣr æt hām wunað’ is ‘where he dwells at home’, with ‘wunað’ in the present although the story is in the past; Thorkelin read ‘wunode’, and Klaeber keeps the present. ‘selfa’ is a nominative, ‘himself’, ‘mid gesīðum’ ‘with companions’, and ‘sǣwealle nēah’ ‘near the sea-wall’, ‘nēah’ taking the dative; ‘sǣweall’ is a bank or cliff-wall by the shore, and the exact picture is a guess.

sentences.t:
Bold wæs betlīc, bregorōf cyning,
heâ healle, Hygd swīðe geong,
sentences.l: The building was fine, the king ruler-bold, in the high hall, Hygd very young,
sentences.i: The dwelling was splendid, its king a bold ruler in his high hall, and Hygd very young,
sentences.n: ‘Bold wæs betlīc’ is ‘the building was fine’: ‘bold’ is a neuter noun, ‘dwelling, hall’, and ‘betlīc’, ‘splendid, stately’, is a word whose sense is a guess. ‘bregorōf cyning’ is ‘the king prince-bold’ (‘brego’ ‘ruler, lord’ and ‘rōf’ ‘brave, strong’); the apparatus shows editors splitting it into ‘brego rōf’ and Trautmann reading ‘beadorōf’, ‘battle-bold’. ‘heâ healle’ is probably ‘in the high hall’, ‘healle’ a dative, and ‘heâ’ a contracted form of ‘hēah’ (the circumflex is Klaeber’s contraction mark); a locative dative without a preposition is rough, and the apparatus lists mendings (‘on hēan healle’, ‘on hēahealle’, ‘hēah on healle’), so the grammar here is not firm. ‘Hygd swīðe geong’ is ‘Hygd very young’, a new name; the next lines call her ‘Hæreþes dohtor’ (1929), and on Klaeber’s reading of 1931–1932 ‘folces cwēn’, queen of the people, is she as well, so she is Higelac’s wife in the house just described; the next unit’s notes show that this reading is itself disputed.

sentences.l: wise, well-grown, though few of winters within the burg-enclosures she has lived through, Hæreth’s daughter;
sentences.i: wise and well-accomplished, though she has lived only a few winters within the stronghold, Hæreth’s daughter;
sentences.n: ‘wīs wēlþungen’ is ‘wise, well-grown’, two nominatives for Hygd: ‘wēlþungen’ is the past participle of ‘þēon’, ‘thrive, excel’, with ‘wēl’ ‘well’, so ‘well-developed, accomplished’. ‘þēah ðe … gebiden hæbbe’ is ‘though she has lived through’, ‘hæbbe’ a present subjunctive after ‘þēah ðe’ and ‘gebiden’ the participle of ‘gebīdan’, ‘live through, experience’ (Thorkelin and Trautmann read ‘hæfde’, the past, as the story is). ‘wintra lȳt’ is ‘few of winters’, ‘lȳt’ ‘little’ taking the genitive plural ‘wintra’. ‘under burhlocan’ is ‘within the burg-enclosures’: ‘burhloca’ is the enclosure of a stronghold (‘burh’ ‘stronghold’ and ‘loca’ ‘enclosure’, cf. ‘locene’ at 1890), and ‘burhlocan’ is a weak form, dative singular or accusative plural. The phrase may mean her time since marriage or her years in all, and the English keeps both open. ‘Hæreþes dohtor’ is ‘Hæreth’s daughter’, ‘Hæreþes’ a genitive.

sentences.t:
næs hīo hnāh swā þēah,
nē tō gnēað gifa Gēata lēodum,
māþmgestrēona.
sentences.l: Not was she niggardly, however, nor too sparing of gifts to the Geats’ people, of treasure-possessions.
sentences.i: She was not mean, for all that, nor too sparing of gifts to the Geat people, of treasures.
sentences.n: ‘næs hīo hnāh’ is ‘she was not niggardly’: ‘næs’ is ‘ne wæs’, ‘hīo’ ‘she’, and ‘hnāh’ means ‘low, mean’, here ‘stingy’. ‘swā þēah’ is ‘however, for all that’. ‘nē tō gnēað’ is ‘nor too sparing’, ‘tō’ with an adjective meaning ‘too’ and ‘gnēað’ ‘sparing, grudging’; ‘gifa’ and ‘māþmgestrēona’ are genitive plurals, ‘of gifts’ and ‘of treasure-possessions’ (‘māþm’ ‘treasure’ and ‘gestrēon’ ‘what is gained, wealth’), the second in apposition to the first, after the adjective, and ‘Gēata lēodum’ is a dative, ‘to the people of the Geats’. A queen was expected to be free with gifts, as Wealhtheow is with the cup (612); the poet praises Hygd by that standard, and then sets a very different queen beside her.

sentences.t:
Mōd Þrȳðe [ne] wæg,
fremu folces cwēn, firen’ ondrysne;
sentences.l: Thryth’s pride she did not bear, the excellent queen of the folk, a dread crime;
sentences.i: The excellent queen of the people did not carry Thryth’s proud spirit, that dreadful wrong;
sentences.n: This is one of the poem’s famous cruces, and the reading is disputed. As Klaeber prints it, ‘wæg’ is the past singular of ‘wegan’, ‘bear, carry’ (here ‘show, practise’), the subject is ‘fremu folces cwēn’, ‘the excellent queen of the folk’, that is Hygd, and the object comes first: ‘mōd Þrȳðe’ is ‘Thryth’s pride’, ‘mōd’ ‘spirit, pride’ and ‘Þrȳðe’ a genitive of the woman’s name, with ‘firen’ ondrysne’ in apposition, ‘a dread crime’. The apostrophe marks a lost final ‘e’ before the vowel, ‘firene ondrysne’, an accusative of ‘firen’ ‘crime’ and ‘ondrysne’ ‘dreadful, fearful’; Chambers suggests that ‘firen’ is masculine here, and others propose ‘firena’, ‘firenum’ or ‘firenon’. The ‘ne’ is Klaeber’s addition (the bracket), following Schücking, and the italic ‘e’ marks another change: the manuscript has ‘mod þryðo wæg’. With ‘ne’ the sentence contrasts Hygd with Thryth; without it, and with the name read as ‘Mōdþrȳðo’ (Kemble, Thorkelin, Grein) ‘Modthryth bore a dread crime’ makes Thryth herself the subject and ‘fremu folces cwēn’ an ironic ‘excellent queen’, which is a natural start for what follows. ‘fremu’ is also uncertain: Bugge and Sedgefield read ‘fre(o)mu’, ‘excellent, vigorous’, nominative singular feminine, which I follow as a guess; Rieger and Trautmann read a noun ‘fremþu’, ‘goodness, benefit’; Cosijn ‘frēcnu’, ‘bold, dangerous’. The sense of ‘mōd Þrȳðe’ and of ‘fremu’ rests on guesses that the grammar does not settle.

sentences.l: None of her own companions, bold though he were, dared venture that, except the great-lord: that he should stare on her with eyes by day;
sentences.i: None of her own companions, however bold, dared risk staring at her by daylight, except her lord;
sentences.n: ‘nǣnig … dorste … genēþan’ is ‘no one dared venture’: ‘dorste’ is the past of ‘durran’, and ‘genēþan’ is ‘venture, risk’; ‘þæt’ stands for the clause that follows, ‘þæt … starede’, ‘that he should stare’, ‘starede’ a past subjunctive of ‘starian’. ‘dēor’ is ‘bold, stern’ (the second part of ‘hildedēor’, 312), describing ‘nǣnig’, and ‘swǣsra gesīða’ is a genitive plural, ‘of her own companions’. ‘Hire’ is Thryth, the woman the poet now describes, with Hygd left behind in the previous sentence. ‘nefne sinfreâ’ is ‘except the great-lord’: ‘nefne’ is ‘except’, ‘sin-’ ‘great, lasting’ and ‘frea’ ‘lord’, the husband (the circumflex is Klaeber’s contraction mark); Grundtvig, Holthausen and Chambers, among others, read two words, ‘sīn frea’, ‘her own lord’. ‘hire an dæges ēagum starede’ is disputed. I take ‘an’ as ‘on’ standing after the pronoun ‘hire’ (‘starede on hire’, ‘stared at her’), ‘dæges’ as ‘by day’ and ‘ēagum’ as ‘with eyes’; Kemble and Thorkelin read ‘āndæges’, ‘daily’, and Munch ‘andēges’, ‘openly’ (compare Gothic ‘andaugjō’), and Holthausen would read ‘hīe’ for ‘hire’. In each reading no one but her husband is said to have looked at her openly or daily.

sentences.t:
ac him wælbende weotode tealde
handgewriþene;
sentences.l: but for him she reckoned appointed death-bonds, hand-twisted;
sentences.i: but for the man who did, she held ordained a deadly binding, twisted by hand;
sentences.n: ‘ac him’ is ‘but for him’, the man who dared to look, ‘him’ a dative. ‘wælbende’ is ‘death-bonds’ (‘wæl’ ‘slaughter, the slain’ and ‘bend’ ‘bond’), accusative plural, and ‘handgewriþene’ ‘hand-twisted’ (the participle of ‘gewrīþan’, ‘twist, bind’) agrees with it. The line’s verbs are hard. ‘tealde’ is the past of ‘tellan’, ‘reckon, hold’, with an unexpressed subject, Thryth (see ‘hire’ in the last unit); I take ‘weotode’ as a participle agreeing with ‘wælbende’, ‘appointed, ordained’, so ‘she held the death-bonds appointed for him’; the other possibility is a second past verb, ‘she ordained, she reckoned’ (‘wītian’, ‘appoint’), and both leave the meaning that his fate is fixed. Both 1787 transcripts agree on ‘weotode’, so the doubt is the sense and not the letters. The semicolon is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
hraþe seoþðan wæs
æfter mundgripe mēce geþinged,
sentences.l: quickly afterwards, after the hand-grip, was it settled by sword,
sentences.i: and soon after the seizure by hand it was settled with the sword,
sentences.n: ‘hraþe seoþðan’ is ‘quickly afterwards’. ‘wæs … geþinged’ is an impersonal passive, ‘it was settled’, ‘geþinged’ being the participle of ‘geþingian’, ‘settle, appoint, decree’, with no subject named, so what is settled is the man’s fate. ‘æfter mundgripe’ is ‘after the hand-grip’, ‘mundgripe’ a dative (‘mund’ ‘hand’ and ‘gripe’ ‘grasp’), the seizing of the man by hands and bonds, as at 753, of the grip Grendel met. ‘mēce’ is the dative of ‘mēce’, ‘sword’, and ‘mēce geþinged’ has two readings: ‘settled by the sword’, which I follow, or ‘appointed to the sword’; either way the man dies by the blade.

sentences.t:
þæt hit sceādenmǣl scȳran mōste,
cwealmbealu cȳðan.
sentences.l: that it the divided-marked blade might shear, might make known death-bale.
sentences.i: so that the patterned sword might cut it through and deal out deadly harm.
sentences.n: ‘þæt hit sceādenmǣl scȳran mōste, cwealmbealu cȳðan’ is the result clause. ‘mōste’ is a past of ‘mōtan’, ‘be allowed, may’ (a subjunctive here after ‘þæt’, though the past singular looks the same in the indicative), and takes two infinitives. I take ‘sceādenmǣl’ as the subject (nominative neuter) and ‘hit’ as the thing it acts on, ‘it’, the matter or the man; this is a guess, since the word order could be read the other way and the pronoun has no clear antecedent. ‘sceādenmǣl’ occurs only here: ‘mǣl’ is ‘mark’ and so a marked or patterned sword (as in the ‘ring-marked’ blade of 1521 and the ‘twist-patterned’ one of 1531), and ‘sceāden’ is the past participle of ‘scēadan’, ‘divide, part’, giving ‘divided-marked’, a pattern in separate bands, which is a guess. ‘scȳran’ I take as ‘shear, cut’, a figure for cutting the matter short; the lexica do not give the sense firmly. ‘cwealmbealu’ is ‘death-bale’ (‘cwealm’ ‘death’ and ‘bealu’ ‘evil, harm’), the object of ‘cȳðan’, ‘make known, show’, so ‘deal out deadly harm’.

sentences.t:
Ne bið swylc cwēnlīc þēaw
idese tō efnanne, þēah ðe hīo ǣnlicu sȳ,
þætte freoðuwebbe fēores onsǣce
æfter ligetorne lēofne mannan.
sentences.l: Not is such a queenly custom for a lady to perform, though she be peerless, that a peace-weaver should assail of life a dear man after a lie-offence.
sentences.i: It is no queenly custom for a lady to practise, however matchless she may be, that a peace-weaver should take the life of a dear man over a pretended offence.
sentences.n: ‘Ne bið swylc cwēnlīc þēaw idese tō efnanne’ is ‘such is not a queenly custom for a lady to carry out’: ‘swylc’ ‘such’ agrees with ‘þēaw’ ‘custom’, ‘idese’ is a dative, ‘for a lady’, and ‘tō efnanne’ an inflected infinitive, ‘to perform’ (several editors read the plain ‘efnan’). ‘þēah ðe hīo ǣnlicu sȳ’ is ‘though she be peerless’: ‘ǣnlicu’ is a nominative feminine, ‘matchless, unique, beautiful’ (from ‘ān’ ‘one’), and ‘sȳ’ a present subjunctive of ‘bēon’. The clause after ‘þætte’ is the deed: ‘freoðuwebbe’ is a nominative, ‘peace-weaver’ (‘freoðu’ ‘peace’ and ‘webbe’ ‘weaver’, a feminine noun), a word for a woman whose marriage is meant to knit two peoples together, and a title of a queen; it occurs only here in the poem, and I take it as the subject of ‘onsǣce’. ‘fēores onsǣce’ is ‘should assail of life’: ‘onsǣce’ is a present subjunctive, which I take as ‘assail, attack’, ‘fēores’ a genitive of ‘fēorh’, ‘life’, and the manuscript has ‘on sæce’, two words, which Kemble, Rieger and others join as ‘onsēce’; Klaeber prints ‘onsǣce’. ‘æfter ligetorne’ is ‘after a lie-offence’ (‘lyge’ ‘lie’ and ‘torn’ ‘anger, injury’), a word that occurs only here, and ‘a pretended offence’ is a guess. ‘lēofne mannan’ is ‘a dear man’, an accusative.

sentences.t: Hūru þæt onhōhsnod[e] Hemminges mǣg:
sentences.l: Indeed that Hemming’s kinsman checked:
sentences.i: Hemming’s kinsman, at any rate, put a stop to that:
sentences.n: ‘onhōhsnod[e]’ is a hard word. The manuscript has ‘on hohsnod’, and Thorkelin added the ending, which Klaeber puts in brackets, ‘onhōhsnode’, a past singular. The lexica give the verb ‘onhōhsnian’ as ‘check, hinder, put a stop to’, perhaps from ‘hōh’, ‘heel, hock’, so that it first meant ‘hamstring’; that origin is a guess, and ‘check’ is the sense I give. ‘þæt’ is its object, ‘that’, the queen’s cruelty, and ‘Hūru’ is ‘indeed, at any rate’. ‘Hemminges mǣg’ is ‘Hemming’s kinsman’ (‘mǣg’ ‘kinsman’): the manuscript has ‘hem ninges’, and Klaeber’s italic ‘m’ marks his joining and altering of it to ‘Hemminges’ (Kemble, Müller and Sievers do the same; Grein and Sievers once printed ‘Hēminges’). He is not named here; from the next lines he is Offa, and the same phrase is used of ‘Ēomēr’ at 1961, which suggests Hemming was a forebear of both. That identification is a guess. The colon introduces another version of the story.

sentences.t:
ealodrincende ōðer sǣdan,
þæt hīo lēodbealewa lǣs gefremede,
inwitnīða, syððan ǣrest wearð
gyfen goldhroden geongum cempan,
sentences.l: ale-drinkers said otherwise, that she did less of people-evils, of malicious hatreds, after first she was given, gold-adorned, to a young warrior,
sentences.i: The ale-drinkers told it otherwise: that she did less harm to the people, less of malice and hatred, from the time she was first given, gold-adorned, to a young warrior,
sentences.n: ‘ealodrincende’ is a present participle used as a noun, ‘ale-drinking ones’, nominative plural, the men at the bench who pass the tale along; ‘ōðer’ is ‘otherwise’ and ‘sǣdan’ the plural past of ‘secgan’, ‘said’. ‘þæt hīo … gefremede’ is the content of what they said, ‘gefremede’ a past subjunctive of ‘gefremman’, ‘do, commit’, in reported speech. ‘lǣs’ is ‘less’ and takes the genitive plurals ‘lēodbealewa’ (‘of people-evils’, ‘lēod’ ‘people’ and ‘bealu’ ‘evil’, a word found only here) and ‘inwitnīða’ (‘of malicious hatreds’, the ‘inwitnīþas’ of 1858). ‘syððan ǣrest wearð gyfen’ is ‘after first she was given’, ‘wearð gyfen’ a passive, and ‘goldhroden’ ‘gold-adorned’ describes her; ‘geongum cempan’ is a dative, ‘to a young warrior’. So the tale is that her marriage made her gentler.

sentences.l: dear in noble birth, after she Offa’s hall over the fallow flood, by her father’s counsel, on the journey sought;
sentences.i: a man precious in his birth, after she, at her father’s bidding, had crossed the pale sea to Offa’s hall;
sentences.n: ‘æðelum dīore’ describes the young warrior, ‘dear in noble birth’, ‘æðelum’ a dative plural of ‘æðelu’, ‘noble descent’. ‘syððan hīo … gesōhte’ is ‘after she sought’: ‘gesōhte’ is the past of ‘gesēcan’, ‘seek out, go to’, ‘Offan flet’ its object, ‘Offa’s hall’ (‘flet’ ‘floor, hall’; ‘Offan’ a genitive), and ‘sīðe’ a dative, ‘on the journey’. ‘ofer fealone flōd’ is ‘over the fallow flood’, ‘fealu’ meaning ‘pale, yellow-brown’, said of the sea, so she crosses water to reach her husband. ‘be fæder lāre’ is ‘by her father’s counsel’, ‘be’ with a dative and ‘lār’ ‘teaching, counsel’, so the marriage was her father’s arrangement. The man named here is Offa.

sentences.t:
ðǣr hīo syððan well
in gumstōle, gōde mǣre,
līfgesceafta lifigende brēac,
sentences.l: where she afterwards well, on the man-seat, good, famed, of her life’s allotments, living, had the use,
sentences.i: where afterwards, good and renowned, she enjoyed well, while she lived, the life that was allotted her, on her throne,
sentences.n: ‘ðǣr’ is ‘where’, the hall of Offa; ‘hīo … brēac’ is ‘she enjoyed’, ‘brēac’ the past of ‘brūcan’, which takes the genitive, here ‘līfgesceafta’, a genitive plural, ‘of life’s decrees’ (‘līf’ ‘life’ and ‘gesceaft’ ‘decree, what is ordained’, so the portion of life allotted to her). ‘lifigende’ is a present participle, ‘living’, agreeing with ‘hīo’, ‘while she lived’. ‘in gumstōle’ is ‘on the man-seat’ (‘guma’ ‘man’ and ‘stōl’ ‘seat’), the high seat or throne. ‘gōde mǣre’, ‘good, famed’, describe her, in what I take to be weak feminine nominative forms. ‘well’ is taken with ‘brēac’, ‘enjoyed well’, though it could also go with ‘in gumstōle’; ‘syððan’ is ‘afterwards’.

sentences.t:
hīold hēahlufan wið hæleþa brego,
ealles moncynnes mīne gefrǣge
þone sēlestan bī sǣm twēonum,
eormencynnes;
sentences.l: she held high-love toward the ruler of heroes, of all mankind, by my hearing, the best between the seas, of the whole race of men;
sentences.i: she held a high love for the lord of warriors, the best of all mankind, as I have heard, anywhere between the seas, in the whole race of men;
sentences.n: ‘hīold hēahlufan wið hæleþa brego’ is ‘she held high love toward the lord of heroes’: ‘hīold’ is the past of ‘healdan’, ‘hēahlufan’ (‘hēah’ ‘high’ and ‘lufu’ ‘love’) its object, ‘wið’ takes the accusative ‘brego’, ‘ruler, lord’, and ‘hæleþa’ is a genitive plural, ‘of heroes’; the lord is Offa. ‘þone sēlestan’ is ‘the best’ in apposition to ‘brego’, with the partitive genitives ‘ealles moncynnes’ (‘of all mankind’) and ‘eormencynnes’ (‘of the whole race’, ‘eormen-’ ‘vast, universal’ as in ‘eormengrund’ at 859). The italic ‘one’ marks a change: the manuscript has ‘þæs’, a genitive that would not agree with the accusative ‘brego’, and Thorkelin’s ‘þone’ is printed. ‘mīne gefrǣge’ is ‘by my hearing’, as I have heard, the poet’s usual way of citing report (776, 837). ‘bī sǣm twēonum’ is ‘between the seas’, the poem’s phrase for the whole known world (858–859).

sentences.t:
forðām Offa wæs
geofum ond gūðum, gārcēne man,
wīde geweorðod,
sentences.l: for Offa was, by gifts and by wars, a spear-bold man, widely honoured,
sentences.i: for Offa, a man bold with the spear, was honoured far and wide for his gifts and his wars,
sentences.n: ‘forðām’ is ‘for, because’, giving the reason for the praise just given. ‘Offa wæs … geweorðod’ is ‘Offa was honoured’, a passive with the participle ‘geweorðod’ and ‘wīde’ ‘widely’; ‘geofum ond gūðum’ are datives plural, ‘by gifts and by wars’, the two things a king was honoured for, giving and fighting. ‘gārcēne man’ is ‘a spear-bold man’ (‘gār’ ‘spear’ and ‘cēne’ ‘bold’), in apposition to ‘Offa’.

sentences.t:
wīsdōme hēold
ēðel sīnne; —
sentences.l: with wisdom he held his homeland; —
sentences.i: and with wisdom he ruled his native land.
sentences.n: ‘wīsdōme hēold ēðel sīnne’ is ‘with wisdom held his homeland’: ‘wīsdōme’ is a dative, ‘with wisdom’, ‘hēold’ the past of ‘healdan’ in the sense ‘hold, rule’, ‘ēðel’ ‘homeland, native land’ its object, and ‘sīnne’ an accusative masculine of ‘sīn’, ‘his own’. The dash that follows is Klaeber’s, and marks the turn from Offa to his descendant in the next line.

sentences.t:
þonon Ēomēr wōc
hæleðum tō helpe, Hem[m]inges mǣg,
nefa Gārmundes, nīða cræftig.
sentences.l: Thence Eomer sprang, to heroes for help, Hemming’s kinsman, nephew of Garmund, skilled in strife.
sentences.i: From him sprang Eomer, to be a help to warriors, Hemming’s kinsman, Garmund’s nephew, mighty in battle.
sentences.n: ‘þonon’ is ‘from there, from him’, so Eomer comes of Offa; ‘wōc’ is the past of ‘wacan’, ‘arise, be born’, ‘hæleðum tō helpe’ ‘to heroes for help’, a dative plural and a dative. The name is an emendation, which Klaeber marks with the italic ‘Ē’: the manuscript has ‘geomor’, ‘sad, gloomy’, which leaves the verb without a subject, and Thorkelin proposed the name ‘Ēomēr’ (Bachlechner ‘Ēomǣr’). ‘Hem[m]inges mǣg’ is ‘Hemming’s kinsman’, repeated from 1944, with the second ‘m’ added in brackets because the manuscript has ‘hem inges’ (Kemble, as the apparatus says, has ‘mm’). ‘nefa Gārmundes’ is ‘nephew of Garmund’, ‘nefa’ a nominative that can mean ‘nephew’ or ‘grandson’, ‘Gārmundes’ a genitive; if Eomer is Offa’s son, ‘grandson’ and Garmund as Offa’s father would fit, but the lines do not say so. ‘nīða cræftig’ is ‘skilled in strife’, ‘nīða’ a genitive plural and ‘cræftig’ ‘skilled, strong’.
